blocks.text: We are well familiar with various types of waves such as water waves in the ocean and circular ripples formed on a still pool of water by rain drops. When a musician plucks a guitar string, sound waves are generated in air which reach our ear and produces sensation of music. The vast energy of the Sun, millions kilometres away, is transferred to the Earth by light waves. In this chapter, we will discuss, formation, propagation and applications of different types of waves.

A wave is a regular disturbance or variation that carries energy, which spreads out from the source. For example, energy is transferred from the Sun to the Earth in the form of light waves called electromagnetic waves, can even travel through vacuum. However, in a medium, energy is transferred due to the regular and repeated disturbances that travel through the medium, making its particles to move up and down or back and forth (to and fro). Imagine a stone thrown into a pond of water (Fig. 7.1).

items: The stone produces a disturbance (ripple) that travels through the water (medium).
The water particles move up and down at their own places, creating a repeating pattern known as wave that spreads out.

blocks.text: The waves can be described by the following parameters:

items: Amplitude (A): The maximum displacement of the wave (or particles of the medium) from its equilibrium position.
Frequency (f): The number of oscillations/vibrations or cycles per second.
Wavelength (λ): The distance between two consecutive similar points on the wave that are in phase.
Period (T): The time taken by the wave to complete one oscillation or cycle. it is the reciprocal of the frequency T = 1/f.

Types of Waves
Waves have various forms, each with unique characteristics. A brief detail of different types of waves is given below:
1. Mechanical Waves

These waves require a physical medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to propagate. Examples are water waves (ocean, lake, or pond ripples), sound waves (audible vibrations in air, water, or solids), seismic waves (earthquakes), etc.
2. Electromagnetic Waves

They do not require a medium to propagate and therefore, can travel through vacuum. Examples are radiowaves (wireless communication), Microwaves (cooking and heating), Infrared waves (IR or heat radiation), Visible light (sunlight, lamp light), Ultraviolet waves (UV radiation), X-rays (medical imaging), Gamma rays (high-energy radiation), etc.
3. Quantum Waves
Quantum waves are associated with particles like electrons and photons. Examples are matter waves/particle waves (electron waves in atoms) or de-Broglie waves, photon waves (light quanta), etc.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: These wave types are essential to understand various phenomena in physics, engineering, and everyday life.
4. Surface Waves
Surface waves propagate along surfaces or interfaces between two mediums. Examples are ocean surface waves (wind-driven waves), seismic surface waves, etc.
Transverse and Longitudinal Waves

There are two main types of waves which are named as transverse waves and longitudinal waves. A transverse wave is one in which the vibrations of the particles are at right angle to the direction in which the energy of the wave is travelling. Whereas a longitudinal wave is one in which the direction of the vibration of the particles is along or parallel to the the direction in which the energy of the wave is travelling.
The transverse wave and longitudinal wave are illustrated in Figs. 7.3 (a and b), respectively.

blocks.alt: (a) Transverse waves: a hand on the left moves a long spring lying on a table sideways (up-down arrows on the handle); the spring forms a wave that travels right, arrow labelled Wave, to the Fixed end. (b) Longitudinal waves: the hand pushes and pulls the spring along its length (left-right arrows); compressions and stretched parts move along it to the Fixed end.
